80	- `app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/promote/cancel/page.tsx` — static cancel page.
81	- `app/[locale]/publica/PromoteUpsellModal.tsx` — the modal, colocated like
82	  `PublishAuthGate.tsx` / `CompleteProfileGate.tsx` in the same route folder.
83	- `app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/components/EventPromoteAction.tsx` — owner-only "Promote"
84	  entry point on the event detail page itself, mirroring `EventEditAction.tsx` exactly
85	  (client-side `useAuth()` check, `ownerId`/`slug` props, no extra round-trip). Gerard's
86	  own description of the flow starts with "hi hagi un botó de promocionar esdeveniment...
87	  a la pàgina d'esdeveniment" — the modal is the *post-publish* upsell path, this is the
88	  *always-available* path for an owner revisiting their own event later. Missing this
89	  was a scope gap caught in review.
90	- `app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/page.tsx` — render `EventPromoteAction` next to
91	  `EventEditAction` (wherever that already renders — same sidebar/mobile-detail slot).
92	
93	**Modified**
94	- `lib/api/events.ts` — new `createPromotionCheckout(id: string, successUrl: string,
95	  cancelUrl: string): Promise<{ url: string }>`, same shape as
96	  `updateEventById`/`deleteEventById`: `requireMutationAuth()` for the Bearer token,
97	  `fetchWithHmac` with `skipBodySigning: true`, POST to
98	  `${apiUrl}/events/${id}/promotions/checkout` with `{ successUrl, cancelUrl }` as the
99	  JSON body (see "Return pages" for why the frontend, not the backend, builds these).
100	  Throws on failure — the Server Action wrapping it is what converts that into a

106	  from the authenticated user already available via `useAuth()` in this file. Around line

110	- `lib/api/events.ts` (`createE2EEvent`) — set `owner: extras?.owner` on the constructed
111	  E2E event object.

118	  bypasses the `/api/*` HMAC gateway entirely (same as `createEventAction`). No
119	  allowlist/middleware change needed. (Verified: the one place in this codebase where a
120	  browser-initiated mutation to `/api/events/*` exists — `DELETE /api/events/[slug]` —
121	  needed an explicit regex carve-out in `gateApiRequest`. The Server Action route avoids
122	  that class of change entirely.)
123	- No new `app/api/*` route. No Stripe SDK/webhook/secret in this repo for this feature.

125	## Modal (Wallapop-style)
126	
127	Reuses the shared `Modal` component (`components/ui/common/modal`) unchanged, but its
128	close/navigate sequencing must be exact:
129	
130	- **"Promote Event"** is the modal's `actionButton`. Its `onActionButtonClick` handler
131	  calls `router.push('/e/${slug}/promote')` and then **explicitly returns `false`**.
132	  This matters: `Modal` (`components/ui/common/modal/index.tsx:92-102`) calls
133	  `setOpen(false)` automatically after `onActionButtonClick` resolves, *unless* the
134	  handler returns `false`. Without the explicit `return false`, the sequence would be:
135	  push to `/promote` → Modal's own `setOpen(false)` still fires on the (now unmounting,
136	  or about-to-unmount) component → in practice this is a redundant state update racing
137	  the navigation, not a correctness bug per se, but it's exactly the escape hatch Modal
138	  documents for "don't auto-close, I'm handling it" — using it here removes the race
139	  entirely rather than relying on unmount timing to save us.
140	- **"Keep it free"** is a plain button inside the modal body (not wired through
141	  `actionButton`) → calls `setOpen(false)` then `router.push('/e/${slug}')` directly
142	  (today's existing post-publish behavior, unchanged).
143	- Backdrop/back-arrow dismiss falls back to the same "keep it free" path (`setOpen`'s
144	  default `onClose` already routes there) — no separate analytics event for that edge,
145	  matching how the existing preview modal in the same file already behaves.
146	
147	Copy (from the brief): "Boost your event! Promote your event now to reach way more
148	people and appear at the top of the platform." Exact translated strings live in
149	`messages/*.json` under `App.Publish.promoteUpsell.*`.
150	
151	## Checkout flow
152	
153	**Server Action signature and ownership check.** Copied verbatim from the pattern in
154	`app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/edita/actions.ts` (`editEvent(eventId, slug, data)`), which
155	exists precisely to prevent a client from passing an `eventId` it doesn't actually own
156	alongside a `slug` it does:
157	
158	```ts
159	type PromotionCheckoutResult =
160	  | { success: true; url: string }
161	  | { success: false; error: string };
162	
163	async function createPromotionCheckoutAction(
164	  eventId: string,
165	  slug: string,
166	): Promise<PromotionCheckoutResult>
167	```
168	
169	Inside the action: resolve `event` via `fetchEventBySlug(slug)`, resolve `currentUser`
170	via `getCurrentUser()`, reject (`{ success: false, error: ... }`) unless `event.id ===
171	eventId` **and** `currentUser?.id === event.owner?.id` — both checks, exactly as
172	`editEvent` does at lines 24-47. `PromoteEventClient` therefore needs both `event.id` and
173	`event.slug` as props from the Server Component (`page.tsx` already has both from the
174	same `fetchEventBySlug` call the ownership gate already uses).
175	
176	**The action returns a result, it does not throw.** `createPromotionCheckout` (the
177	`lib/api/events.ts` function) throws on non-2xx and on `requireMutationAuth()` failure —
178	same as `updateEventById`/`deleteEventById`. But unlike those two (which are called from
179	contexts that already handle thrown errors upstream), this Server Action is the last
180	stop before the client needs to render an error state, so it must catch and convert,
181	exactly like `createEventAction` does for `createEvent`'s 401/403 throws. This is not
182	optional: since Gerard's endpoint doesn't exist yet, a 404 (or any non-2xx) *is* the
183	realistic near-term demo path, and an uncaught throw from a Server Action reaches the
184	client as an opaque, Next.js-redacted rejection in production — not the "generic inline
185	error" this design promises.
186	
187	**Building the request:** the action builds `successUrl`/`cancelUrl` itself (see "Return
188	pages" below for why) using `siteUrl` (`@config/index`) + `withLocalePath` + the known
189	`slug`, then calls `createPromotionCheckout(event.id, successUrl, cancelUrl)` → `POST
190	${apiUrl}/events/${id}/promotions/checkout` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and
191	`{ successUrl, cancelUrl }` as the JSON body → `{ url }`.
192	
193	**Client-side redirect, with validation.** `PromoteEventClient` calls the action, and on
194	`{ success: true, url }` **validates `url` before redirecting** — it must parse as an
195	absolute `https://` URL (matching the precedent in `uploadEventImage`,
196	`lib/api/events.ts:489-498`, which validates its own returned URL rather than trusting it
197	blindly). This guards two real failure modes at once: a provisional/renamed backend field
198	silently producing `window.location.href = "/undefined"`, and an unvalidated redirect
199	target becoming an open-redirect surface. If validation fails, treat it the same as a
200	`{ success: false }` result — generic inline error, no partial redirect attempt.
201	
202	No assumption is made about Gerard's error response shape/codes (none confirmed) — any
203	non-2xx surfaces as the same one generic inline error on the promote page ("Something
204	went wrong, try again"), no special-casing by status code.
205	
206	## Return pages
207	
208	`/e/[eventId]/promote/success` and `/e/[eventId]/promote/cancel`, static, mirroring the
209	existing `/patrocina/success` + `/patrocina/cancelled` precedent (feature-scoped, not
210	global). Per Stripe's own docs (confirmed via web search of stripe.com/docs): "customers
211	aren't guaranteed to visit the success page" — fulfillment must come from the webhook,
212	never the redirect. Since that webhook lives in Gerard's Spring Boot backend, these pages
213	do zero verification; they are purely "thank you" / "canceled, event stays free" copy
214	with a link back to the event.
215	
216	**`success_url` / `cancel_url` are built by this app, not the backend, and sent in the
217	checkout POST body.** This reverses the original assumption in this design's first draft.
218	Reasoning: `/e/[eventId]/promote/success` uses `[eventId]` as a **slug** (confirmed —
219	this route param is a slug throughout the app, resolved via `fetchEventBySlug`; see the
220	canonical-slug `redirect()` logic in `app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/page.tsx`), plus a locale
221	prefix. The backend only ever receives the UUID (`event.id`) in the checkout request path
222	— it has no way to construct a slug-based, locale-prefixed URL like
223	`/es/e/estiu-al-carrer-2026/promote/success` from that UUID alone. So the frontend
224	computes both absolute URLs (via `siteUrl` + `withLocalePath` + the known `slug`) and
225	passes them to the backend as part of the checkout request; the backend's Stripe session
226	creation uses whatever it's given rather than constructing its own.
227	
228	## Analytics (new)
229	
230	Matching the existing `publish_*` naming already in `app/[locale]/publica/page.tsx`,
231	sent via `sendGoogleEvent` (imperative calls, matching the majority pattern in that file
232	— not the declarative `data-analytics-*` attribute pattern used inside `EventForm`):
233	
234	- `promote_modal_shown` — `{ event_slug, source: "publica" }`
235	- `promote_modal_cta_click` — `{ event_slug, source: "publica" }`
236	- `promote_modal_dismiss` — `{ event_slug, source: "publica" }`
237	- `promote_page_view` — `{ event_slug, source: "promote" }`
238	- `promote_checkout_click` — `{ event_slug, source: "promote" }`
239	- `promote_checkout_redirect` — `{ event_slug, source: "promote" }` (fired right before
240	  the `window.location.href` redirect to Stripe; named `_redirect` rather than
241	  `_success` since no payment has happened yet at this point — actual payment success is
242	  only known to the backend via its webhook)
243	- `promote_checkout_error` — `{ event_slug, source: "promote", reason }`
244	
245	## Testing
246	
247	- Unit (Vitest): `createPromotionCheckout` and `createPromotionCheckoutAction` — env-guard
248	  + HMAC call shape, ownership-mismatch rejection, and the throw-to-result conversion.
249	  (Correction from an earlier draft of this doc: `updateEventById`/`deleteEventById`
250	  don't have dedicated unit tests today — they're exercised indirectly via mocks in
251	  `test/server-actions.test.ts` and `test/api-events-slug-cache.test.ts`. The new
252	  functions should get real direct unit tests, not just mocked call-sites, since this is
253	  a money-adjacent path.) Modal button branching (Promote vs. Keep it free navigate to
254	  the right paths, and the `actionButton` handler's `return false` is asserted so the
255	  race described above can't regress silently).
256	- E2E (Playwright): **this requires two changes to E2E infra, not just a new
257	  assertion.**
258	  1. `createE2EEvent` (`lib/api/events.ts`) never sets `owner`, so the new promote page's
259	     ownership gate would `notFound()` for every E2E-created event regardless of who's
260	     logged in. Fix: extend `E2EEventExtras` with `owner`, populate it in
261	     `buildE2EExtras()` (`publica/page.tsx`) from the already-authenticated E2E test
262	     user, and pass it through in `createE2EEvent`.
263	  2. `e2e/publish-integration.spec.ts`'s existing assertion
264	     (`page.waitForURL((url) => !url.pathname.includes("/publica"), ...)` right after
265	     clicking publish) currently races the new modal: the URL no longer changes on
266	     publish success, the modal appears instead. This existing test **must be updated**,
267	     not just extended — insert an explicit wait for the modal, then a "Keep it free"
268	     click, before the existing URL assertion can proceed. Add a second, separate test
269	     (or a branch in the same one) that instead clicks "Promote Event" and asserts landing
270	     on `/e/[slug]/promote`.
271	
272	## Risks / open questions carried forward (not blocking this implementation)
273	
274	- Real endpoint contract may differ once Gerard ships it (field names, auth, error
275	  shape, and whether it even accepts `successUrl`/`cancelUrl` in the body as this design
276	  assumes). Mitigated by isolating the call in one function
277	  (`createPromotionCheckout`) and by the client-side URL validation described above.
278	- Pricing is a hardcoded placeholder; will need a real config once Gerard's pricing
279	  methodology is decided.
280	- "Appears at top of list" has no frontend implementation — purely a backend ranking/
281	  endpoint decision still pending on Gerard's side.
282	- The existing preview-modal path in `publica/page.tsx` (`showPreview` →
283	  `onActionButtonClick` → `await onSubmit()`) already relies on the publish button's
284	  existing `isLoading`/spinner state (via `isPending` from `useTransition`) to cover the
285	  time between form submission and the new upsell modal appearing — this is pre-existing
286	  behavior this design relies on rather than changes, and is called out here so it isn't
287	  mistaken for an oversight if the gap is ever felt during a demo.
288	
289	## Review history
290	
291	This design went through one adversarial staff-engineer review pass (2026-08-03) before
292	implementation. Five blocking issues were found and fixed in this document: (1) the
293	modal's `actionButton` auto-close racing the "Promote Event" navigation — fixed by an
294	explicit `return false`; (2) the Server Action signature couldn't support an ownership
295	check with only `eventId` — fixed by adding `slug` and copying `editEvent`'s
296	double-check; (3) the action was designed to let `createPromotionCheckout` throw through
297	to the client — fixed with a discriminated result type; (4) `success_url`/`cancel_url`
298	can't be built from a UUID alone since the return routes use slugs — fixed by having the
299	frontend build and pass both URLs to the backend; (5) the existing E2E publish test and
300	`createE2EEvent`'s missing `owner` field would break/block the new promote-page
301	assertions — fixed by extending E2E test infra and explicitly updating (not just
302	extending) the existing test. All five are reflected in the sections above, not just
303	listed here.
304

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/albertolive/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

  see `.github/workflows/e2e-integration.yml`), not the mocked-auth or
  `E2E_TEST_MODE`-short-circuited specs (`publish-wizard.spec.ts`,
  `publish-no-autosubmit.spec.ts`, `publica_to_event.flow.spec.ts` — none of those
  submit-and-land-on-`/e/[slug]`, so they're unaffected). Its existing assertion
  (`page.waitForURL((url) => !url.pathname.includes("/publica"), ...)` right after
  clicking publish) races the new modal: the URL no longer changes immediately on
  publish success, the modal appears instead. This existing test **must be updated**,
  not just extended — insert an explicit wait for the modal, then a "Keep it free"
  click, before the existing URL assertion can proceed. Add a second, separate test (or
  a branch in the same one) that instead clicks "Promote Event" and asserts landing on

  publishes a real event, `event.owner` is populated by the backend itself — no
  synthetic E2E owner-stamping is needed for the new promote page's ownership gate to

## Review history

This design went through one adversarial staff-engineer review pass (2026-08-03) before
implementation. Five blocking issues were found and fixed in this document: (1) the
modal's `actionButton` auto-close racing the "Promote Event" navigation — fixed by an
explicit `return false`; (2) the Server Action signature couldn't support an ownership
check with only `eventId` — fixed by adding `slug` and copying `editEvent`'s
double-check; (3) the action was designed to let `createPromotionCheckout` throw through
to the client — fixed with a discriminated result type; (4) `success_url`/`cancel_url`
can't be built from a UUID alone since the return routes use slugs — fixed by having the
frontend build and pass both URLs to the backend; (5) the existing E2E publish test and
`createE2EEvent`'s missing `owner` field would break/block the new promote-page
assertions — fixed by extending E2E test infra and explicitly updating (not just
extending) the existing test. All five are reflected in the sections above, not just
listed here.

## Review history

This design went through one adversarial staff-engineer review pass (2026-08-03) before
implementation. Five blocking issues were found; four are fixed in this document as
written: (1) the modal's `actionButton` auto-close racing the "Promote Event" navigation
— fixed by an explicit `return false`; (2) the Server Action signature couldn't support
an ownership check with only `eventId` — fixed by adding `slug` and copying `editEvent`'s
double-check; (3) the action was designed to let `createPromotionCheckout` throw through
to the client — fixed with a discriminated result type; (4) `success_url`/`cancel_url`
can't be built from a UUID alone since the return routes use slugs — fixed by having the
frontend build and pass both URLs to the backend.

The fifth (E2E test breakage) needed a follow-up correction after the review: the
reviewer's proposed fix — extending `E2EEventExtras`/`createE2EEvent` with a synthetic
`owner` field — turned out to be solving a problem that doesn't exist for the one test
that's actually affected. `e2e/publish-integration.spec.ts` (the only spec that publishes
and asserts on the post-publish redirect) authenticates against the real staging backend
and publishes a real event, so `event.owner` is already populated server-side; the
mocked-auth/`E2E_TEST_MODE` specs that *would* need a synthetic owner
(`publish-wizard.spec.ts`, `publish-no-autosubmit.spec.ts`,
`publica_to_event.flow.spec.ts`) never submit-and-land-on-`/e/[slug]`, so they're
unaffected by the modal either. Verified directly against all four spec files before
finalizing — see "Testing" above for the corrected, narrower fix (update the one race
condition in `publish-integration.spec.ts`, no E2E infra changes).

543	---
544	
545	## Overview
546	
547	A neighborhood noticeboard rendered with the polish of a modern app. The
548	core job is helping people in Catalonia decide what to do today, this
549	weekend, or near a town they're visiting — so every screen is a thin frame
550	around event imagery and a few decisive details (date, place, price). Chrome
551	retreats; the photography and the listings carry the page.
552	
553	The voice is local and unhurried. Copy is sentence-case, human, and lightly
554	multilingual (Catalan first, with Spanish and English). The visual system is
555	quiet enough to host hundreds of cards in a row without fatigue, and warm
556	enough that a single event detail page still feels like an invitation rather
557	than a database record.
558	
559	The aesthetic targets are *civic*, *warm*, *photographic*, *content-first*,
560	*native*, and *Mediterranean*. Reference points are GitHub and Facebook for
561	system-font pragmatism, Airbnb-style event grids for soft shadows and
562	generous gutters, and the Catalan flag's senyera red for brand confidence.
563	
564	## Colors
565	
566	One brand color does almost all the work: a confident Catalan red,
567	intentionally darkened from a brighter `#FF0037` to **`#D6002F`** so it
568	clears WCAG AA against white (≈ 5.2:1). It marks calls-to-action, the active
569	state on filters, the focus glow, hyperlink hovers on the footer's agenda
570	grid, and the price accents on cards. A deeper variant `#A80025` handles
571	pressed and hover states. A 31%-alpha "primary-soft" wash is the only
572	acceptable way to use red as a fill on light surfaces — used for date-range
573	middles, soft glows, and active chip tints.
574	
575	Everything else is neutral. The canvas is true `#FFFFFF`; chrome and
576	disabled fills sit on `#F7F7F7`. Body text is **`#454545`** — never pure
577	black — which gives the page a slightly softer, paper-like cast and pairs
578	naturally with the warm red. Headings and form labels go to true black for
579	hierarchy. Borders are `#CCCCCC` at full strength but more often appear at
580	20–60% alpha as hairlines that frame cards without competing with them.
581	
582	Status colors (success green, warning amber, error red, info blue) are
583	imported from a conventional palette and are *only* used for their meaning —
584	never decoratively. Success green appears on free or discounted price
585	labels; warning amber on "few seats left" / soon-to-expire urgency; error
586	red on validation; info blue is reserved for system notices.
587	
588	The hero is the one place the palette flips. There, full-bleed documentary
589	photography sits under a **60% black overlay** (`#00000099`), white type
590	carries `text-shadow`, and inactive filter chips take on a glassmorphic look
591	— `#FFFFFF26` fill with an 8px backdrop blur and a `#FFFFFF4D` border that
592	brightens on hover. The active filter chip drops the glass and goes solid
593	red with a leading checkmark.
594	
595	Contrast budget: body on white ≈ 7.5:1 (AAA); primary on white ≈ 5.2:1
596	(AA); muted-foreground on white ≈ 4.6:1 (AA). No token below AA is used for
597	text.
598	
599	## Typography
600	
601	The product uses the **system font stack** — `-apple-system`,
602	`BlinkMacSystemFont`, `Segoe UI`, `Roboto`, `Helvetica Neue`, `Arial` — same
603	as Facebook, GitHub, Instagram, and Twitter. There are no webfonts to load,
604	no FOUT, no licensing overhead. The trade-off is intentional: a civic,
605	community-built product should feel native to whatever device the reader is
606	on rather than imposing a brand voice through letterforms.
607	
608	Because system fonts hint and render slightly stronger than custom display
609	faces, weights are tuned conservatively: **400** for body, **500** for nav
610	labels and small UI, **600** for headings (semibold), **700** only for the
611	hero H1. `font-synthesis` is disabled so we never get a smeared faux-bold.
612	
613	The type scale follows a four-level heading model:
614	
615	- **heading-1** (24/700 mobile → 36/700 desktop) — page identity, one per
616	  page, typically the hero greeting.
617	- **heading-2** (20/600 mobile → 24/600 desktop) — major section dividers.
618	- **heading-3** (18/600 mobile → 20/600 desktop) — subsections, category
619	  headers.
620	- **heading-4** (16/500 mobile → 18/500 desktop) — card titles, footer
621	  block titles.
622	
623	UI chrome — nav links, footer links, button labels — uses a small **label**
624	style: 12/500, **uppercase**, with widened tracking. This is the one place
625	the type design speaks loudly, and it gives buttons their characteristic
626	civic-poster confidence. A `label-tight` (11/600) is reserved for category
627	badges on cards.
628	
629	Body inputs are pinned to **16px** to defeat iOS Safari's focus auto-zoom.
630	
631	## Layout
632	
633	A mobile-first canvas with a clean expansion at 768px. The page uses four
634	container widths:
635	
636	- **page** (1280px) — the outermost cap.
637	- **article** (896px) — long-form pages, terms, privacy.
638	- **form** (672px) — focused vertical spines for forms and settings.
639	- **detail** (520px) — the event detail spine.
640	
641	Vertical rhythm is anchored by `spacing.3xl` (48px) for major section
642	breaks, with `spacing.2xl` (32px) and `spacing.4xl` (64px) variants.
643	Horizontal gutter is `spacing.lg` (16px) until **lg**, where the gutter
644	drops to 0 and the container is centered. A `spacing.sticky-offset` of
645	128px reserves space below the fixed search/filter bar on listing pages so
646	the first row of cards never slides under the chrome.
647	
648	Cards live in a responsive grid: 1 column on mobile, 2 on **sm**, 3 on
649	**md+**, with `spacing.md` (12px) between cells. Card titles use a 2-line
650	clamp and a fixed `min-height` so adjacent cards visually align even when
651	titles vary.
652	
653	Z-layers are explicit: 10 sticky chrome, 100 dropdowns, 900 modals, 1000
654	tooltips. Anything above 1000 is forbidden.
655	
656	Navigation is a top sticky bar on desktop, a fixed bottom tab bar on mobile
657	— a deliberate native-app affordance for a product that's used walking
658	around towns. The desktop bar is 56px tall with a backdrop blur and a
659	hairline border. The mobile bar is 64px tall with five circular icon-only
660	buttons (Home, Agenda, Favorites, Publish, News), each at least 44×44 px;
661	the active route fills with `colors.primary-tint` and tints its icon
662	primary red.
663	
664	## Elevation & Depth
665	
666	Shadows are deliberately soft. They use the body color (`#454545`) at low
667	alpha rather than pure black, with short y-offsets and modest spreads, so
668	they sit kindly on warm white. Cards default to a **hairline border + no
669	shadow**; on hover the border tightens and a small `elevation.md` shadow
670	blooms. Modals get `elevation.lg`. The hero banner gets `elevation.xl`.
671	Anything beyond `xl` is forbidden.
672	
673	Focus is communicated as a **3-pixel `#D6002F33` glow ring** plus, on
674	critical actions, a 2-offset solid ring. Errors swap red for the
675	`elevation.focus-error` red. Focus is *always* communicated, but only on
676	`:focus-visible` so mouse-clicking doesn't leave a ring trail.
677	
678	The hero photograph carries the highest depth in the system: a `60%` black
679	overlay sits between the image and the type. Below that, glassmorphic chips
680	add a second layer of depth via `backdrop-filter: blur(8px)` over the
681	photograph itself. Outside the hero, blur is never used.
682	
683	## Shapes
684	
685	The platform's signature gesture is the **full-pill button** —
686	`rounded.full` (`9999px`) — applied to primary, outline, ghost, neutral, and
687	category buttons alike. Pills paired with a cherry-red fill read as
688	confident and a touch festive without tipping into playful, which is the
689	tonal target.
690	
691	Cards and content containers use **`rounded.md`** (12px). Inputs settle at
692	**`rounded.sm`** (8px); modals and the rich-text editor sit at
693	**`rounded.lg`** (16px). Badges and chips share the button's full-pill
694	shape. There are no sharp 90° corners anywhere except inside the
695	date-picker's range-middle days (intentional — it stitches the range
696	visually).
697	
698	The card image area is a strict **3:2 ratio** with a `surface-muted`
699	placeholder for slow networks. The hero image is full-bleed, anchored to
700	`object-position: center 60%` to keep faces in frame on portrait crops.
701	
702	## Components
703	
704	**Buttons** are full pills, always uppercase label text. Primary is solid
705	red on white; outline is a 2px red border that fills on hover; neutral is a
706	2px gray border that shades; ghost is fill-only-on-hover; category is the
707	softer chip variant for filter-style picks. Pressing translates the button
708	1px down with a hint of scale-down (0.995) — fast, 100ms. Disabled buttons
709	drop to 50% opacity and lock the cursor.
710	
711	**Cards** are an article tile: 3:2 image on top, category pill, then a
712	muted metadata row (`date · time · price · multi-day`), a 2-line title, and
713	finally a location row anchored to the bottom with a pin icon. The whole
714	tile is a clickable article element with the link absolutely positioned to
715	cover the card. Hovering tightens the border and zooms the image to 1.03
716	over 300ms. The favorite button overlays the image in the top-right and
717	heart-beats (1 → 1.15 → 1) on activation.
718	
719	**Chips** have two contexts: on-light (white fill, hairline border, hover
720	shades to muted) and on-photo (glassmorphic over hero photography). The
721	active variant in on-photo flips to solid red with a leading check icon.
722	
723	**Tab bar** is a count-over-label navigation strip (e.g. profile Propers /
724	Passats), not a client-side tabpanel switch — each item is a link to its own
725	route. A full-width hairline rail (`border-border`) carries items with a
726	2px bottom border; the active item's border goes solid red with
727	`foreground-strong` text, inactive items sit at `foreground/80` on a
728	transparent border. The count renders above the label in `heading-3`,
729	label below in `body-small`. Wrapped in the horizontal-scroll primitive on
730	narrow screens so it never breaks the rail's height.
731	
732	**Empty states** (e.g. "no events yet") center a title + description with
733	generous vertical padding (`spacing.3xl`) and an optional primary-pill CTA
734	below. Title uses `heading-3` in `foreground-strong`; description sits in
735	regular `foreground`.
736	
737	**Modals** on mobile take the full `100dvh` and read like a screen, not a
738	popup; on **sm+** they cap at 500px wide with a 16px-radius card. Header is
739	sticky (back arrow + centered uppercase title), footer is sticky and
740	safe-area-inset aware (single primary action button, full width). The
741	backdrop is the scrim color at 60%.
742	
743	**Inputs** are 40px tall by default (48px in `input-large`), 8px corners,
744	`#CCCCCC` border. Focus glows red, error glows feedback-error. Range slider
745	thumbs are 24-px circles in primary red.
746	
747	**Date picker** is a high-touch primitive: red selected days as solid
748	circles, a 6–8% red wash for range middles, a 35%-alpha red dashed border
749	on "today", and red chevrons. Days are 28×28 (filter context) or 36×36
750	(form context). Focus rings always render — even when `outline: none` is
751	set on the day button — via box-shadow.
752	
753	**Footer** is a long, generous tower: a soft white→muted gradient, a social
754	row, a centered nav strip, a sponsor CTA card, a 2/3/4-column grid of
755	"agenda for [town]" links, and finally the copyright + tagline. Hr dividers
756	between blocks are 50%-alpha hairlines. The agenda links use a 4-px
757	underline-offset and a 2-px decoration thickness on hover — a quiet but
758	specific link signature.
759	
760	**Navigation progress bar**: a 3px primary-red bar at the top of the page
761	during client-side route changes, replacing the spinner pattern.
762	
763	**Motion**: the default easing is `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)`. A
764	`bounce-subtle` easing exists but is reserved for confirmations —
765	favoriting an event, copying a share link. View Transitions fade the page
766	root: 90ms ease-in out, 210ms ease-out in (delayed 90ms). Every transition
767	collapses to 0ms under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.
768	
769	## Do's and Don'ts
770	
771	**Do**
772	
773	- Use `colors.primary` only for genuine calls-to-action, active states,
774	  focus, and price/price-free accents. Treat it as a scarce resource.
775	- Pair white type over photography with a `text-shadow` and a 60% overlay
776	  — never bare white on raw photography.
777	- Default cards to a hairline border and *no* shadow. Let shadow bloom on
778	  hover only.
779	- Pin form inputs to 16px+ to prevent iOS auto-zoom.
780	- Use `:focus-visible` (not `:focus`) for all focus rings.
781	- Keep mobile interactive targets at 44×44 px minimum.
782	- Mark hero subtitles with `data-speakable="description"` so voice
783	  surfaces can extract them.
784	- Use sentence case for body and metadata. Reserve UPPERCASE for buttons,
785	  nav labels, and small UI chrome.
786	- Use semantic feedback colors for their meaning only (success on free
787	  prices, warning on urgency, error on validation, info on system notes).
788	
789	**Don't**
790	
791	- Don't introduce a second brand color. The Catalan red is the system's
792	  only chromatic accent.
793	- Don't use `colors.primary` as a large fill behind body text; only at
794	  31% alpha or below for tints.
795	- Don't use pure black (`#000000`) for body copy. Body is `#454545`.
796	- Don't add webfonts. The system stack is a feature, not a placeholder.
797	- Don't introduce gradient meshes, mascots, or illustrated artwork. The
798	  imagery direction is documentary photography of Catalan culture.
799	- Don't ship dark mode tokens. The system is light-only by intent.
800	- Don't exceed `elevation.xl` shadows. There is no `elevation.2xl`.
801	- Don't synthesize bold weights — `font-synthesis` stays disabled.
802	- Don't use `bounce-subtle` easing for navigation, hovers, or page
803	  transitions. Reserve it for confirmation gestures only.
804	- Don't use blur outside the hero / photographic surfaces.
805	- Don't break the canonical hover pattern on cards (border tightens +
806	  shadow blooms + image scales 1.03). Stay consistent across the grid.
807

**Types — one real miss**
- `PromotionCheckoutResult` sits in `types/props.ts` in my plan. Wrong file. `EditEventResult` and `CreateEventActionResult` — the two direct precedents this type is modeled on — both live in `types/event.ts`. Should move there.

- I used `heading-1`, `card-bordered`, `btn-primary`, `body-large` etc. — all real classes, I just re-verified them in `styles/globals.css`. Good long-term question, and there's a real fork here I want to flag before we lock anything in.

**The reuse opportunity that actually matches this:** the sponsor system (`/patrocina`) already has almost exactly this shape — `config/pricing.ts` keys prices by `${duration}:${geoScope}` (town/region/country), and there's even a second, currently-disabled pattern built for event-scoped promotions (`/api/promotions/config` + `/api/promotions/price-preview`, in `RestaurantPromotionForm.tsx`) that fetches available durations/scopes and a live price preview from the backend rather than hardcoding them in the frontend. That second pattern is the durable one — it means the frontend doesn't need to know the pricing matrix at all, it just asks the backend "what are my options and what do they cost," and renders whatever comes back.

**But there's a real conceptual gap, not just a pricing one.** Sponsor "geoScope" answers *which page shows a banner* — a placement decision. Event "geoScope" for boosting reach answers something structurally different: *should a Cardedeu event start appearing in Barcelona-region or all-Catalonia event listings it wouldn't normally match*. That's not a pricing tier, that's a change to how `/api/events?place=X` decides what belongs in a listing — a query/ranking concern on Gerard's side, not something this frontend can simulate by picking a tier. Duration (1 day, this weekend, 3 weeks) is comparatively easy — it's just "how long does `paid` stay true" — but the geo axis needs Gerard to actually decide it works before we design UI for it, the same way pricing methodology is still undecided.

**My recommendation:** don't hardcode the flat €5 as a dead-end constant. Build the promote page today to call a `config` + `price-preview` pair (mirroring the existing restaurant-promotion pattern, new endpoints Gerard would own), even if right now that config only ever returns one duration and one scope. That way, when he adds real duration options and decides whether geo-scope boosting is even feasible, the frontend gains a selector without a rewrite — it's the same "ask the backend what's available" shape, just with more options in the response. The €5 flat price stays as today's *only* returned option, not a frontend-owned assumption.

Want me to sketch what that config-driven promote page looks like (still MVP-scoped, no selector UI yet, just the right seam for one to slot in later), or do you want to nail down the geo-scope question with Gerard first before designing anything further?
yes

Here's the honest architecture answer, and it splits into two very different problems.

**Duration is Gerard's problem, not ours — and he told us that directly.** His own words: "jo tindria que tindre aquests preus jo a base de dades" (I'd need to have these prices in a database myself) and price appears after "jo calcularia el preu" (I would calculate the price). The frontend never sends a price or a duration to him — it sends `eventId` + return URLs, and he computes and returns a number. That means we structurally cannot build a duration picker today, because we'd be inventing options and prices he hasn't defined. Any picker we ship now is a guess dressed up as a feature. The safe long-term move is to keep the checkout call exactly as already planned — no price/duration fields in the request — and treat "what are the duration options and their prices" as a question to put back to him, not something to architect around blind.

**Geo-scope is a different animal, and it's not actually a pricing tier at all.** "Boost to my town vs. region vs. all Catalonia" isn't a checkout option, it's a change to how `/api/events?place=barcelona` decides an event belongs there. Right now a Cardedeu event only surfaces in Cardedeu/Vallès Oriental listings because of its own `city`/`region` fields — nothing in the query layer has a concept of "this event is externally boosted into a listing it doesn't naturally belong to." That's a backend ranking/query decision, and notably, it's not in Gerard's voice note at all. He only described "appear at the top" (sort order within its natural listing) and a possible future "give me the promoted ones" endpoint — never expanding an event's geographic reach. That's a good idea, but it's a new idea, not confirmed scope.

So the actual long-term shape I'd propose, and what I'd bring back to Gerard as concrete questions rather than build blind:

1. Is duration ever a user choice, or does the backend decide it automatically (e.g., "stays paid until the event happens")?
2. If it is a user choice, what are the actual options and how does price map to them — because we can't invent that table, only he can.
3. Is "reach a wider area" (town → region → Catalonia) something he's even considered, or does "promoted" just mean "sorts first in its existing town/region"? That's a scope question for him, not a design question for us.

Nothing in the current implementation plan needs to change to stay compatible with this. The Server Action already sends nothing but `eventId` + return URLs — no invented price/duration params to unwind later. What I'd do differently right now, cheaply: keep `EVENT_PROMOTION_FLAT_FEE_EUR` in `config/pricing.ts` exactly as planned, but comment it clearly as "the only price until Gerard defines tiers," so whoever revisits this later knows it's a placeholder with a known follow-up, not a design decision. I would not build any selector UI, local or fake-fetched, until his answer comes back — building it now risks the same rewrite-when-wrong problem as guessing the checkout contract itself.

Want me to draft the exact questions above into a short message you can send Gerard, or leave it as-is and proceed with executing the current plan while that conversation happens in parallel?

**Config-driven price fetch, not hardcoded constant.** Instead of `PromoteEventClient` importing `EVENT_PROMOTION_FLAT_FEE_EUR` directly from `config/pricing.ts`, it should call a small internal API route (`GET /api/promotions/event-config` or similar) that today returns exactly one option — `{ options: [{ id: "standard", price: 5, currency: "eur", durationLabel: "..." }] }` — and renders whatever it gets back as a single selected card. If Gerard later adds duration/geo tiers, that same endpoint starts returning multiple entries in `options[]`, and the UI's job becomes "render N selectable cards instead of 1" — a genuine additive change, not a rewrite. This mirrors the exact pattern already proven in `RestaurantPromotionForm.tsx` (`/api/promotions/config` + `/api/promotions/price-preview`), so it's not a new idea for this codebase, just applied to events instead of restaurants.

**The checkout Server Action stays exactly as planned** — no price or duration in the request, only `eventId` + `successUrl`/`cancelUrl`. Whatever tier the user picks (today: none, there's only one) gets resolved server-side by Gerard, same as now.

# Executing Plans

## Overview

Load plan, review critically, execute all tasks, report when complete.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the executing-plans skill to implement this plan."

**Note:** Tell your human partner that Superpowers works much better with access to subagents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, Copilot CLI, and Gemini CLI all qualify; see the per-platform tool refs in `../using-superpowers/references/`). If subagents are available, use superpowers:subagent-driven-development instead of this skill.

## The Process

### Step 1: Load and Review Plan
1. Ensure an isolated workspace: use superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one
2. Read plan file
3. Review critically - identify any questions or concerns about the plan
4. If concerns: Raise them with your human partner before starting
5. If no concerns: Create todos for the plan items and proceed

### Step 2: Execute Tasks

For each task:
1. Mark as in_progress
2. Follow each step exactly (plan has bite-sized steps)
3. Run verifications as specified
4. Mark as completed

### Step 3: Complete Development

After all tasks complete and verified:
- Announce: "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch
- Follow that skill to verify tests, present options, execute choice

## When to Stop and Ask for Help

**STOP executing immediately when:**
- Hit a blocker (missing dependency, test fails, instruction unclear)
- Plan has critical gaps preventing starting
- You don't understand an instruction
- Verification fails repeatedly

**Ask for clarification rather than guessing.**

## When to Revisit Earlier Steps

**Return to Review (Step 1) when:**
- Partner updates the plan based on your feedback
- Fundamental approach needs rethinking

**Don't force through blockers** - stop and ask.

## Remember
- Review plan critically first
- Follow plan steps exactly
- Don't skip verifications
- Reference skills when plan says to
- Stop when blocked, don't guess
- Never start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Ensure work happens in an isolated workspace. Prefer your platform's native worktree tools. Fall back to manual git worktrees only when no native tool is available.

**Core principle:** Detect existing isolation first. Then use native tools. Then fall back to git. Never fight the harness.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Step 0: Detect Existing Isolation

**Before creating anything, check if you are already in an isolated workspace.**

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
```

## Step 1: Create Isolated Workspace

**You have two mechanisms. Try them in this order.**

### 1a. Native Worktree Tools (preferred)

The user has asked for an isolated workspace (Step 0 consent). Do you already have a way to create a worktree? It might be a tool with a name like `EnterWorktree`, `WorktreeCreate`, a `/worktree` command, or a `--worktree` flag. If you do, use it and skip to Step 2.

Native tools handle directory placement, branch creation, and cleanup automatically. Using `git worktree add` when you have a native tool creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage.

Only proceed to Step 1b if you have no native worktree tool available.

### 1b. Git Worktree Fallback

**Only use this if Step 1a does not apply** — you have no native worktree tool available. Create a worktree manually using git.

#### Directory Selection

Follow this priority order. Explicit user preference always beats observed filesystem state.

1. **Check your instructions for a declared worktree directory preference.** If the user has already specified one, use it without asking.

2. **Check for an existing project-local worktree directory:**
   ```bash
   ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
   ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
   ```
   If found, use it. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

3. **If there is no other guidance available**, default to `.worktrees/` at the project root.

#### Safety Verification (project-local directories only)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:** Add to .gitignore, commit the change, then proceed.

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

#### Create the Worktree

```bash
# Determine path based on chosen location
path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"

git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

**Sandbox fallback:** If `git worktree add` fails with a permission error (sandbox denial), tell the user the sandbox blocked worktree creation and you're working in the current directory instead. Then run setup and baseline tests in place.

# PR Review Loop

Run AI code review to convergence on one PR, hands-off. One round = fetch → evaluate →
fix/decline → resolve → request re-review → wait. Loop rounds until diminishing returns.

This skill is **repo-agnostic**. The mechanics (gh GraphQL, bot triggers, the loop) are
universal. Project-specific judgment is NOT hardcoded here — see "Adapt to the project".

## Round cap and termination

Stop the loop when ANY of these is true:
- A round produces **no new agreed fixes** (every new thread is a decline, or there are zero new unresolved threads).
- The new threads only **repeat already-declined** suggestions from a prior round.
- **5 rounds** have run (safety cap — report that the cap was hit, don't silently continue).

When stopping, report a final table: rounds run, fixed vs declined per round, and which condition ended the loop.

## Step 1 — Identify the PR

```bash
export GH_PAGER=cat
# Use the number if the user gave one; otherwise detect from the branch:
PR=$(gh pr view --json number --jq .number)
REPO=$(gh repo view --json owner,name --jq '"\(.owner.login)/\(.name)"')
```

If no PR exists for the branch, stop and tell the user to create one first (don't create it silently).

### Request Copilot's review (once, at the start)

Unlike the comment-triggered bots, GitHub Copilot is requested as a *reviewer* via the API. Do
it once when the loop starts (it then re-reviews on each push):

```bash
gh api --method POST "/repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/requested_reviewers" \
  -f "reviewers[]=copilot-pull-request-reviewer[bot]"
```

A `200` adds `Copilot` to the PR's requested reviewers and it reviews shortly after. A `422`
means Copilot code review isn't enabled for the repo/org (or the plan doesn't cover it) — note
it and carry on with the other bots, don't let it break the loop. Copilot posts inline review
comments, so Step 3 picks them up as threads with author `Copilot` and Step 4 evaluates them
like any other bot.

## Step 2 — Adapt to the project (do this once, at the start)

Before evaluating suggestions, learn this repo's conventions so declines are grounded:
- The current repo's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` are usually already in context — use them.
- Look for a project review skill (e.g. `code-review-evaluation`) under `.github/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, or `.agents/skills/`. If present, load it — it lists conventions external bots don't know (import rules, type organization, routing/searchParams restrictions, env-var rules, etc.).
- If the repo documents nothing relevant, fall back to generic review judgment (below).

The point: a suggestion that contradicts a documented project convention is a **decline with a reason**, not a fix.

## Step 3 — Fetch unresolved threads

```bash
export GH_PAGER=cat
gh api graphql -f query='
{
  repository(owner: "OWNER", name: "REPO") {
    pullRequest(number: PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first: 50) {
        nodes {
          id
          isResolved
          comments(first: 1) {
            nodes { createdAt author { login } path line body }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' --jq '.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved == false) | {id, author: .comments.nodes[0].author.login, path: .comments.nodes[0].path, line: .comments.nodes[0].line, created: .comments.nodes[0].createdAt, body: .comments.nodes[0].body[0:300]}'
```

No unresolved threads on round 1 → report "no open suggestions" and stop.

## Step 4 — Evaluate each suggestion

Default verdicts (override with project conventions from Step 2):

| Category | Default | Action |
|----------|---------|--------|
| Bug / error / edge-case fix (null check, try/catch, mkdir) | AGREE | Fix |
| Missing docs / fields | AGREE | Fix |
| Unused code / imports | AGREE | Fix |
| Extract constant / reduce duplication | AGREE | Fix |
| Performance (batch calls, avoid N+1) | AGREE | Fix |
| Security (generic patterns) | AGREE | Fix |
| Pattern / architecture change | CHECK PROJECT | Decide against repo conventions |
| Cosmetic refactor of working code | DECLINE | Resolve with rationale |
| Contradicts a documented project convention | DECLINE | Resolve, cite the convention |
| Repeat of a previously declined suggestion | DECLINE | Resolve, reference prior round |

Present a summary table before changing anything:

```
| # | Source | Line | Issue | Verdict |
|---|--------|------|-------|---------|
| 1 | Gemini L594 | Batch API calls | ✅ AGREE — N calls → 1 |
| 2 | Cubic L88   | Don't exit on error | ❌ DECLINE — CI needs to fail loud |
```

## Step 5 — Apply fixes, then resolve all threads

Read flagged sections (parallel reads), make minimal fixes, then validate with whatever the
repo uses (`yarn typecheck && yarn lint`, `npm test`, etc. — check package.json / Makefile).

One commit per round:

```bash
git add <files>
git commit -m "fix: address AI review feedback (round N)

- <fix 1> (Source)
- <fix 2> (Source)"
git push || (git pull --rebase && git push)
```

Resolve ALL threads (fixed **and** declined) in one loop:

```bash
for TID in "THREAD_ID_1" "THREAD_ID_2"; do
  gh api graphql -F tid="$TID" -f query='mutation($tid: ID!) {
    resolveReviewThread(input: {threadId: $tid}) { thread { isResolved } }
  }' --jq '.data.resolveReviewThread.thread.isResolved'
done
```

## Step 6 — Trigger the next review (only if needed)

The push in Step 5 already re-triggers most bots: CodeRabbit re-reviews incrementally on new
commits, and Gemini Code Assist usually re-syncs on push. **Check the repo's bot config — if
it auto-reviews on push, skip the manual trigger.** Only post one if the bot needs it:

```bash
gh pr comment PR_NUMBER --body "Round N: <fixes>. Declined: <rationale>.

@gemini review"
```

Triggers, when needed: `@gemini review`, `@coderabbitai review`, `@cubic-dev-ai review`
(it's `@gemini review`, not `/gemini review`).

Copilot doesn't watch for comment triggers — re-request it as a reviewer instead (re-requesting
also forces a fresh pass even if it would otherwise skip an incremental push):

```bash
gh api --method POST "/repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/requested_reviewers" \
  -f "reviewers[]=copilot-pull-request-reviewer[bot]"
```

## Step 7 — Wait for the new review, then loop

The bot posts a few minutes after the push. Don't busy-hold the session — schedule a single
re-check with `ScheduleWakeup` (~4 min) so the session is free meanwhile; one wake per round.
On wake, re-run Step 3 (compare thread `createdAt` against your push time so you don't
re-process old threads):

- New actionable threads → round N+1, back to Step 4.
- Nothing new after the wake → diminishing returns, stop.

If running interactively and the user prefers to drive the cadence, just report the round and
let them re-invoke when the new review lands — same loop, user-paced.

## Checklist

- [ ] `export GH_PAGER=cat` before GraphQL calls
- [ ] Requested Copilot's review at the start (and re-requested each round), or noted the 422 if it's unavailable
- [ ] Loaded project conventions (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / project review skill) before evaluating
- [ ] Summary table before changes each round
- [ ] Validated fixes (typecheck/lint/test per the repo)
- [ ] `git push` falls back to `--rebase` on rejection
- [ ] Resolved ALL threads, fixed and declined
- [ ] Round number in commit and comment
- [ ] Skipped the manual bot trigger if push already re-reviews; scheduled a single wake to re-check
- [ ] Stopped on no-new-fixes / repeats / 5-round cap, and reported why

result.output:
---
name: code-review-evaluation
description: Evaluate external PR suggestions (Gemini, CodeRabbit) against project conventions. Use when asked to review or agree with external code review comments.
---

# Code Review Evaluation Skill

## Purpose

Evaluate external code review suggestions (Gemini, CodeRabbit, etc.) against project conventions. These tools have access to our codebase and often make valid suggestions - but they don't know our **project-specific conventions**.

## What External Reviewers ARE Good At

CodeRabbit, Gemini, etc. **can see your code** and are excellent at catching:

- ✅ **Missing fields** in examples/docs (like missing `geoScope` in docstring)
- ✅ **Type mismatches** and inconsistencies
- ✅ **Unused imports/variables**
- ✅ **Potential null/undefined errors**
- ✅ **Security vulnerabilities** (generic patterns)
- ✅ **Documentation gaps**
- ✅ **Test coverage suggestions**
- ✅ **General best practices** (accessibility, performance)

**These suggestions are usually VALID - agree with them!**

## What External Reviewers DON'T Know

They lack context about our **project-specific conventions**:

- ❌ Our `@i18n/routing` Link requirement
- ❌ Our `/types` directory governance
- ❌ Our three-layer API proxy pattern
- ❌ Our design system semantic classes
- ❌ Our env variable 4-location rule
- ❌ Our $300 searchParams incident history

**Only check skills when suggestion involves these patterns.**

## Evaluation Framework

When user asks "Do you agree with this suggestion?":

### Step 1: Categorize the Suggestion

| Category            | Examples                                   | Default Response  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------- |
| **Bug/Error fix**   | Missing field, type error, null check      | Usually **AGREE** |
| **Documentation**   | Missing JSDoc, outdated example            | Usually **AGREE** |
| **Code quality**    | Unused code, simplification                | Usually **AGREE** |
| **Code complexity** | >100 lines/function, >10 props, >3 nesting | Usually **AGREE** |
| **Pattern change**  | Different import, new abstraction          | **CHECK SKILLS**  |
| **Architecture**    | Component structure, API calls             | **CHECK SKILLS**  |

### Step 2: If Pattern/Architecture → Cross-Reference Skills

Only check skills if the suggestion involves patterns we have rules for:

| Skill                          | Check For                                           |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `pre-implementation-checklist` | Does suggestion duplicate existing code?            |
| `type-system-governance`       | Does it create types outside `/types`?              |
| `react-nextjs-patterns`        | Does it violate server-first pattern?               |
| `api-layer-patterns`           | Does it bypass three-layer proxy?                   |
| `url-canonicalization`         | Does it add `searchParams` to listing pages?        |
| `i18n-best-practices`          | Does it use `next/link` instead of `@i18n/routing`? |
| `design-system-conventions`    | Does it use `gray-*` or arbitrary utilities?        |
| `env-variable-management`      | Does it add env var without all 5 locations?        |
| `data-validation-patterns`     | Does it skip Zod validation?                        |
| `security-headers-csp`         | Does it use raw `fetch()` without wrappers?         |

### Step 3: Provide Structured Response

## Response Template

```markdown
## Evaluation: [Suggestion Title/Topic]

### Summary

[1-2 sentence summary of the suggestion]

### Category

[Bug fix / Documentation / Code quality / Pattern change / Architecture]

### Skill Check (if pattern/architecture)

- [ ] [Relevant skill] - [Pass/Conflict: reason]

### Recommendation

**[AGREE / DISAGREE / PARTIAL]**

[Explanation]
```

## Example: Valid Suggestion (AGREE)

**CodeRabbit says**: "Docstring example missing geoScope field"

```markdown
## Evaluation: Missing geoScope in docstring

### Summary

Example in JSDoc is missing a required field from the type.

### Category

Documentation - external reviewer caught a real inconsistency.

### Skill Check

Not needed - this is a documentation fix, not a pattern change.

### Recommendation

**AGREE** - The docstring example should match the actual type definition.
```

## Project-Specific Blind Spots (CHECK SKILLS)

Only disagree when suggestion conflicts with our conventions:

### 1. "Use `next/link` directly"

**Our rule**: Always use `Link` from `@i18n/routing`
**Response**: Disagree - breaks locale handling

### 2. "Add types inline in component"

**Our rule**: All types in `/types` directory
**Response**: Disagree - violates type governance

### 3. "Use `gray-500` for text"

**Our rule**: Use semantic tokens (`text-foreground/80`)
**Response**: Disagree - violates design system

### 4. "Add searchParams to page component for filtering"

**Our rule**: NEVER in listing pages (causes $300+ cost spikes)
**Response**: Disagree - violates url-canonicalization (CRITICAL)

### 5. "Use raw fetch() for this API call"

**Our rule**: Use `fetchWithHmac` or `safeFetch`
**Response**: Disagree - violates security patterns

# Event Promotion Checkout (Wallapop-style upsell)

Date: 2026-08-03
Status: Approved for implementation planning

## Problem

Right after a user publishes an event, there's no offer to boost its reach. We want a
post-publish upsell modal (Wallapop-style) leading to a dedicated promotion page, where
confirming payment hands off to Gerard's Spring Boot backend, which owns the Stripe
session, the pending order, and the webhook that activates the promotion. This app's job
is: show the upsell, collect the "yes", get a Stripe URL from the backend, and redirect.

## Source of truth for the backend contract

Gerard (backend, Spring Boot) described the flow directly (verbatim, translated):

> Owner-only for now (not decided if others can promote later). Button on the event page
> → Next.js page → user confirms a price (pricing methodology not decided yet — could be
> per-day, or start-date-to-event-date, TBD) → frontend POSTs to something like
> `api/events/{eventId}/promotions/checkout` → backend validates user + event, computes
> price, creates a PENDING order record, creates a Stripe Checkout Session, returns the
> URL → frontend redirects to Stripe → user pays → Stripe redirects to **our** page
> *and* separately fires a webhook to Spring Boot → webhook flips the order to
> successful and the event to paid → frontend, seeing "paid", would show it promoted —
> or, "we'd build an endpoint to give me the promoted ones" (not decided: a reordered
> list vs. a dedicated endpoint) → a scheduled job later reverts to free at expiry.

This confirms the endpoint shape (`POST /events/{eventId}/promotions/checkout` →
`{ url }`) but confirms nothing else is finalized: pricing methodology, whether
non-owners can promote, and how "promoted" surfaces to the frontend are all explicitly
undecided on the backend side. No OpenAPI spec, staging URL, or Postman collection
exists yet (confirmed with the user). This design treats the endpoint contract as
provisional and isolates it behind a single function so a field-name or shape mismatch,
once the real endpoint ships, is a one-file fix.

## Scope

**In scope**
1. Post-publish upsell modal in `app/[locale]/publica/page.tsx`.
2. `/e/[eventId]/promote` page: benefits, static flat fee (€5, MVP placeholder), "Confirm
   and Pay".
3. Server Action that POSTs to the backend checkout endpoint and returns the Stripe URL
   for the client to redirect to.
4. `/e/[eventId]/promote/success` and `/e/[eventId]/promote/cancel`: static, no
   verification (Stripe's own docs: fulfillment must come from the webhook, not the
   redirect — and that webhook is Gerard's, not ours).
5. Analytics for the funnel.

**Explicitly out of scope**
- Pricing lookup/config — hardcoded constant, marked as MVP-provisional. Gerard: "no sé,
  ja ho pensarem" (pricing methodology not decided).
- Duplicate-checkout / already-promoted guard — no lookup endpoint exists for this yet
  (the closest analog, `/api/promotions/active`, is an explicit `TODO` placeholder for
  an unrelated restaurant-promotion feature and must not be reused here).
- "Appears at top of list" sorting or a "Promoted" badge — no field for this exists on
  `EventSummaryResponseDTO`/`EventDetailResponseDTO`, and Gerard hasn't decided whether
  it's a reordered list or a separate endpoint. Zero changes to list rendering or DTOs.
- Non-owner promotion.
- Any webhook, Stripe SDK usage, or Stripe secret key in this repo. Two other Stripe

## Post-review architecture correction (2026-08-04)

An AI code review pass on the resulting PR (cubic) caught that this design doc and its
implementation plan still described the modal living inside `publica/page.tsx`, but the
shipped code doesn't work that way — a second, user-requested correction moved the modal
after the design doc above was already written. Recording what actually shipped, since a
future reader following the sections above verbatim would build a conflicting flow:

**What actually ships:**
- `publica/page.tsx`'s `onSubmit` success path redirects to `` /e/${slug}?promote=1 ``
  (a query marker, not modal state) instead of rendering the modal itself.
- The modal (`app/[locale]/e/[eventId]/components/PromoteUpsellModal.tsx`) is rendered
  by `EventClient.tsx` — the event's own detail page — gated on `?promote=1` **and** on
  the signed-in user matching `event.ownerId` (a second review finding: without the
  ownership check, any visitor could trigger the upsell by hand-editing the URL, and its
  CTA would lead them to the owner-only `/promote` page, which 404s for them).
- "Keep it free" no longer calls `router.push` at all — the user is already on the
  event's detail page, so it only closes the modal and strips the `promote` query param
  (preserving any other existing params, e.g. `edit_suggested`) via `router.replace`.
- "Promote Event" also strips the `promote` marker (via `router.replace`) *before*
  pushing to `/promote`, so a later browser-back to the event doesn't re-show the modal.
- This reuses the exact one-time-query-marker convention already established by
  `newEvent`/`edit_suggested` in `EventClient.tsx` — not a new mechanism.

**Why the change:** the user's own framing of the request ("when the user creates a new
event, when it lands in the event detail page that has created, appears a new modal")
was the actual product intent all along; the original plan's `publica`-hosted modal
blocked navigation on the publish form itself, which didn't match that.

This correction lives only in this addendum — the "Scope" and "Modal" sections above are
left as historical record of the original plan (each now carries an inline pointer here)
rather than being silently rewritten.
